title: What is anatomy?

refs.capture: p.2 left column: the one paragraph under the heading '1.1 Anatomy and Physiology Defined' (starts 'Two branches of science—anatomy'), which continues at the top of the right column ('with structures of the body, physiology…') for one more paragraph ending with the lung alveoli example; p.2 lower two-thirds: Table 1.1 (whole table, both halves) — the 'Gross anatomy' row in the left half is the definition the slide uses.

basics: Anatomy is the study of what the body is made of and how its parts are arranged in space; physiology is the study of what those parts do. The two are inseparable because shape constrains function (a rigid skull protects, thin-walled air sacs let gas diffuse quickly). 'Gross' anatomy simply means large-scale: what you can see with the naked eye during dissection or on an X-ray, CT or MRI, as opposed to histology (tissue under a microscope). The slide's other bullets are about why a radiographer learns anatomy: pathology (disease changes structure), pharmacology (drugs act on structures) and, above all, a shared vocabulary so that a description like 'lesion in the right upper quadrant' means the same thing to everyone. The slide leaves unsaid that Tortora lists many sub-branches (regional, systemic, surface, imaging, clinical anatomy) in Table 1.1.

title: Levels of structural organization

refs.section_title: Levels of Structural Organization and Body Systems
refs.capture: p.3: Figure 1.1 (the whole-page figure with the six numbered levels, chemical to organismal); p.3 right column: the paragraph under the heading '1.2 Levels of Structural Organization and Body Systems' (starts 'The levels of organization of') plus numbered item 1 'Chemical level', which runs over the page break to p.4 (both columns above Table 1.2: items 2 Cellular, 3 Tissue, 4 Organ, 5 System) and finishes on p.5 left column with item 6 'Organismal level' (one short paragraph below the Clinical Connection box).

basics: The body can be described at six nested scales, each built from the one below. Atoms and molecules (chemical level) assemble into cells, the smallest units that are alive. Cells of similar type plus the material between them form tissues; there are only four basic tissue types: epithelial (coverings and linings), connective (support, binding, transport), muscular (contracts) and nervous (signals). Two or more tissue types combined into a recognisable structure with a job is an organ (stomach, bone, skin). Organs cooperating on one task form a system (digestive, skeletal), and all systems together make the organism. The book's analogy is language: letters, words, sentences, paragraphs, chapters, book. The slide shows the picture only; the point to take away is that 'bone' is an organ (it contains several tissues), while 'bone tissue' is one tissue type — a distinction that matters in Week 1's skeletal slides.

basics: The remaining five systems. Nervous: brain, spinal cord, nerves and sense organs — fast electrical signalling that detects change and commands responses. basics: Every anatomical direction is defined relative to one agreed reference pose, so that 'above' or 'in front of' never depends on how the patient happens to be lying. In the anatomical position the person stands upright, faces the observer, feet flat and forward, arms at the sides with the palms turned forward (so the thumbs point outward). Lying face-down is prone, face-up is supine. Three mutually perpendicular reference planes then slice this posture: a sagittal plane divides left from right (the median or midsagittal plane passes exactly through the midline; a parasagittal plane is off-centre), a coronal (frontal) plane divides front (anterior) from back (posterior), and a transverse (horizontal, axial) plane divides upper (superior) from lower (inferior). A cut along any of these gives a 'section'; CT and MRI images are sections, so the plane names are used daily in imaging. The slide leaves out the oblique plane and the prone/supine terms.

basics: The trunk is not solid: the organs sit inside hollow spaces (cavities) whose walls are bone and muscle. The skull encloses the cranial cavity (brain) and the stacked vertebrae enclose the vertebral canal (spinal cord); these two are continuous. The chest wall and diaphragm enclose the thoracic cavity, which is itself subdivided: a pleural cavity around each lung, the pericardial cavity around the heart, and the mediastinum, the central compartment between the lungs holding heart, great vessels, trachea, oesophagus and thymus. Below the dome-shaped diaphragm is the abdominopelvic cavity, split without any wall into the abdominal part (stomach, liver, intestines, spleen) and the pelvic part (bladder, rectum, reproductive organs). Each of the serous cavities is lined by a slippery double membrane (parietal layer on the wall, visceral layer on the organ) with a film of fluid between, letting organs slide as we breathe. The slide's red grouping into a 'dorsal' and a 'ventral' cavity is a convention from other textbooks.

basics: To say where something is in the abdomen quickly, clinicians draw two imaginary lines through the umbilicus (navel): a vertical median plane and a horizontal transumbilical plane. basics: Directional terms are a coordinate vocabulary; each is a comparison between two structures, not an absolute position, and all assume the anatomical position. Superior/inferior are along the vertical axis (toward the head / toward the feet); the synonyms cephalic or cranial and caudal come from 'head' and 'tail'. Anterior/posterior are along the front–back axis; in humans ventral = anterior and dorsal = posterior (in a four-legged animal they differ). Medial/lateral refer to distance from the midline. Proximal/distal are used only within limbs and mean nearer to / farther from the point where the limb joins the trunk — so the wrist is distal to the elbow whatever the arm is doing. Superficial/deep refer to distance from the skin. Tortora's table adds three the slide omits: intermediate (between two structures), ipsilateral (same side) and contralateral (opposite side), all of which appear in imaging reports.

title: Homeostasis

refs.capture: p.9 left column: the paragraph under the heading '1.4 Homeostasis' (starts 'Homeostasis (hō′-mē-ō-STĀ-sis; homeo- = sameness') — one paragraph with the blood-glucose example; p.9 right column: the two paragraphs under the subheading 'Control of Homeostasis' (start 'Homeostasis in the human body is continually' and 'Fortunately, the body has many') — nervous vs endocrine control.

basics: Homeostasis is the body keeping its internal variables — temperature, blood pH, oxygen, glucose, pressure — inside narrow limits even though the outside world and the body's own activity keep pushing them. It is a dynamic equilibrium: values drift within a band and are continually corrected, which costs energy. Feedback loops do the correcting, with three parts: a receptor that senses the variable, a control centre (brain or endocrine gland) that compares it with a set point, and an effector (muscle, gland, organ) that changes it. In negative feedback the response opposes the original change, so a rise is pushed back down — this is how nearly everything is regulated, and it fades as the variable returns to normal. In positive feedback the response amplifies the change until some outside event breaks the loop (birth, clot completion). Assumed by the slide: signals travel as nerve impulses (fast) or hormones (slow), and 'feedback' means the loop's output alters its input.

title: Child birth

refs.capture: p.12 right column: Figure 1.5 'Positive feedback control of labor contractions during birth of a baby' (whole right half of the page, including the 'Interruption of the cycle' box); text: p.11 right column, last paragraph (starts 'Normal childbirth provides a good'), which runs over the page break to p.13 left column, first paragraph (ends '…oxytocin is no longer released'); p.13 left column, third paragraph (starts 'These examples suggest some important') explains why a positive loop needs an external stop.

basics: Labour is the textbook example of a positive feedback loop. The first uterine contractions push the baby's head against the cervix (the neck of the uterus). Stretch receptors there send more nerve impulses to the brain the more the cervix is stretched; the brain (via the posterior pituitary) releases the hormone oxytocin into the blood; oxytocin makes the uterine muscle contract harder; harder contractions stretch the cervix more — and the cycle escalates. Nothing inside the loop turns it down; it ends only when the baby is delivered and the cervix is no longer stretched, at which point oxytocin release stops. Contrast with negative feedback, which damps itself. The book's other positive-feedback examples are blood clotting (useful) and the downward spiral after severe blood loss (harmful) — positive loops are reserved for rare, self-terminating events.

basics: A bone is an organ built from several tissues (bone tissue, cartilage, marrow, vessels, nerves), and the skeleton as a whole does more than hold us up. Protection: skull round the brain, rib cage round heart and lungs. Blood formation: red marrow inside certain bones manufactures red cells, white cells and platelets (haemopoiesis). Mineral storage: bone holds about 99% of the body's calcium and much of its phosphate and releases them under hormonal control — this is what the slide splits into 'electrolyte balance' and 'acid–base balance' (bone can buffer acid by giving up phosphate and carbonate). Fat storage: yellow marrow is largely fat, a reserve of triglycerides. 'Detoxification' refers to bone sequestering heavy metals such as lead; Tortora does not discuss it.

basics: The adult skeleton has 206 named bones, most of them in left–right pairs. Anatomists split the skeleton in two. The axial skeleton (80 bones) lies along the body's long axis: skull, the tiny ear ossicles, hyoid, vertebral column, sternum and ribs. The appendicular skeleton (126 bones) is everything that hangs off that axis: the arms and legs plus the two girdles (shoulder and pelvic) that attach them. Week 1 covers only the axial half; Week 2 does the appendicular. The slide's '~270 at birth' is a commonly quoted figure but not in Tortora, which just says infants have 'more than 206'.

title: Types of bones based on shape

refs.capture: p.205 lower left: Figure 7.2 'Types of bones based on shape' (long, flat, irregular, short, sesamoid) — the slide reproduces it; text: p.205 left column, the paragraphs under the heading '7.2 Types of Bones' (start 'Almost all bones of the body' — long bones, then 'Short bones are somewhat cube-shaped'), continuing at the top of the right column with 'Flat bones', 'Irregular bones', 'Sesamoid bones' and 'An additional type… Sutural bones' (four paragraphs).

basics: Bones are classified by shape because shape predicts internal structure and job. Long bones (humerus, femur, phalanges) are longer than wide, have a shaft of compact bone and spongy ends, and are slightly curved so load is spread; they act as levers. Short bones (wrist carpals, ankle tarsals) are roughly cubes of spongy bone with a thin compact shell; they transmit force in several directions. Flat bones (skull vault, sternum, ribs, scapula) are two plates of compact bone sandwiching spongy bone — protective shields with a broad surface for muscle attachment. Irregular bones (vertebrae, hip bone, some facial bones) fit none of the above. Sesamoid bones form inside tendons where they rub over bone; the kneecap (patella) is the only constant one, and they improve the tendon's leverage. Tortora adds sutural bones — small extra bones within skull sutures — classified by location, not shape.

basics: Bone is a connective tissue: a few cells embedded in a large amount of extracellular matrix. When an osteoblast walls itself in it becomes an osteocyte, the mature cell that sits in a small cavity (lacuna) and maintains the tissue, exchanging nutrients through tiny channels. basics: At birth the flat bones of the skull vault are not yet joined; between their edges are patches of tough fibrous membrane where bone has not yet formed. basics: The top two cervical vertebrae are specialised for moving the head. Because the ribs tie the thoracic column to the sternum, this is the least mobile part of the spine, which also makes it the region where scoliosis most often shows. basics: The five lumbar vertebrae are the largest and strongest of the free vertebrae because the load carried increases down the column — by L5 they support most of the upper body. The articular facets face medially (superior) and laterally (inferior), interlocking in the sagittal plane; this allows plenty of flexion and extension but almost no rotation. Because it is both heavily loaded and very mobile, the lumbar region is where disc herniation and mechanical back pain are commonest.

basics: The thoracic cage is a bony cone, narrower at the top, flattened front to back, that protects heart, lungs, liver and spleen, supports the shoulder girdle, and moves when we breathe. It has three components. At the back, the twelve thoracic vertebrae. On each side, twelve ribs. Manubrium and body meet at a slight forward angle, the sternal angle, level with the second rib — the landmark from which ribs are counted on a patient. Ribs reach the sternum through bars of hyaline costal cartilage; these cartilage–sternum contacts are the sternocostal joints named on the slide. The gaps between ribs are intercostal spaces, filled by muscle, vessels and nerves.

basics: A joint (articulation) is any place where two bones — or bone and cartilage or teeth — meet, whether or not they move. Anatomists classify joints two ways, and the slide gives both. Functionally, by how much they move: synarthroses do not move, amphiarthroses move slightly, diarthroses move freely. The two schemes roughly line up — fibrous and cartilaginous joints are synarthroses or amphiarthroses, synovial joints are diarthroses — but not perfectly (some synovial joints between carpals barely move). basics: The normal spine has four gentle front-to-back curves and is straight when seen from the front. Three deformities are named by which of these goes wrong. Lordosis ('bent backward') is an exaggerated lumbar curve, the hollow back of late pregnancy, obesity or poor posture. All three are judged on standing radiographs: scoliosis is measured as the Cobb angle on a frontal film, kyphosis and lordosis on a lateral film. The slide gives names only; the book adds causes, signs and treatments.

basics: Between every pair of vertebral bodies from C2 down to the sacrum is a disc: a tough outer ring of fibrocartilage (annulus fibrosus) around a soft, jelly-like, water-rich core (nucleus pulposus). Under load the core is squeezed and the ring bulges, spreading force like a water-filled cushion. Always compressed and without a blood supply, discs degenerate with age: the nucleus dries and the annulus tears. If the posterior ligaments are weak and the annulus gives way, the nucleus can squeeze out — 'herniate' — most often backward and to one side, where it presses on the spinal nerve leaving through the intervertebral foramen (or, higher up, on the cord). Pressure on a root gives pain and weakness in that nerve's territory; lumbar roots feed the sciatic nerve, so pain shoots down the leg. Herniations cluster at L4/5 and L5/S1 because the lumbar spine carries most weight and bends most. MRI shows the bulge; treatment ranges from rest to discectomy.

basics: Each vertebral arch forms from two halves that grow round the spinal cord and fuse in the midline at the laminae. Spina bifida ('split spine') is the congenital failure of that fusion, most often at L5 or S1 where the neural tube closes last. Severity spans a spectrum. Spina bifida occulta: only the bone is open; the skin is intact, perhaps marked by a dimple or tuft of hair, and it is a common incidental finding on radiographs. Meningocele: the meninges (the cord's membranes) and cerebrospinal fluid bulge through the gap as a fluid-filled sac. Meningomyelocele: the cord and nerve roots are in the sac too, so the nerves below the lesion are damaged — leg paralysis, loss of bladder and bowel control, and often hydrocephalus. It is a neural-tube defect, and folic acid supplements before and during early pregnancy sharply cut its incidence; it is detected before birth by maternal blood alpha-fetoprotein and ultrasound.
